big_picture_notes: Ecclesiastes is a poetic-philosophical monologue by Qoheleth framed by a narrator's prologue (1:1-2) and epilogue (12:8-14), forming an inclusio via 'Vanity of vanities! All is vanity.' The central glue is הֶבֶל (hevel) — vanity/breath — alongside refrains such as 'striving after wind,' 'under the sun,' and the positive counter-theme: God's gift to eat, drink, and find enjoyment in toil. Internally, the monologue cycles through a first-person empirical quest (chs. 1–2), broad observations ('I saw...') about times, oppression, wealth, wisdom, and justice (chs. 3–8), and a final exhortation to live wisely in light of certain death (chs. 9–12). Scenes are complete thought-units: poems, proverb clusters, and short essays.

stories.why_start_end_and_literary_glue: A third-person narrator introduces Qoheleth and his thesis (1:1-2) and resumes after the monologue with a summary and orthodox conclusion (12:8-14). Start (1:1): 'The words of the Preacher...' End (12:14): final judgment statement. Literary Glue: narrator's voice and the repeated hevel refrain—'Vanity of vanities! All is vanity'—at 1:2 and 12:8.

scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: The book's frame opens: the words of the Teacher, son of David, and the thesis cry — 'Futility of futilities! Everything is futile.'
The closing inclusio repeats the futility-refrain (8) and praises the Teacher who arranged proverbs like goads from one Shepherd (9-11).
The final word of the whole book: beyond endless books, 'fear God and keep His commandments… for God will bring every deed into judgment.'

stories.why_start_end_and_literary_glue: A first-person, empirical investigation into profit/yitron (1:3–2:26) marked by 'I said/ saw/ made/ applied my heart' and the refrain 'vanity and striving after wind.' Starts with the profit question (1:3) and ends with the first positive refrain of enjoyment as God's gift (2:24-26).

scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: The thesis question 'what does a man gain?' answered by the endless round of generations, sun, wind, and rivers.
All things wearisome, the unsatisfied eye, and the verdict that there is nothing new and no remembrance.

scenes.scene_name: The Quest for Wisdom Is a Miserable Task
scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: The king sets his mind to explore all under heaven — a grievous task, for the crooked cannot be straightened.
Surpassing all before him in wisdom, he learns it too is chasing wind: 'as knowledge grows, grief increases.'
'I will test you with pleasure' — laughter, wine, and folly, while wisdom still guided him, prove futile.
The grand experiment of building: gardens, reservoirs, servants, herds, silver, gold, and singers.

scenes.scene_name: Nothing to Be Gained Under the Sun
scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: Greater than all before him, denying himself no pleasure — yet all his works prove a chasing of wind.

scenes.scene_name: Wisdom and Folly: A Common Fate
scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: Wisdom exceeds folly as light exceeds darkness, yet one fate overtakes both — so he comes to hate life.

scenes.scene_name: The Vanity of Toil Left to Another
scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: Despair over labor that must be handed to a successor who may be a fool — grief even at night.

scenes.scene_name: Enjoyment Is the Gift of God
scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: The first of the book's refrains: nothing better than to eat, drink, and find satisfaction from God's hand.

stories.story_title: The Poem of Times and Observations on Oppression
stories.why_start_end_and_literary_glue: Moves from 'I' experiments to 'I saw/considered' observations, anchored by the 'times' poem (3:1-8). Observes sovereignty, injustice, oppression, envy, solitude, companionship, and political popularity under the sun. Ends with vanity refrain (4:16).

scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: The famous poem opens: a season for everything — born and dying, planting, weeping, and dancing.

scenes.scene_name: A Time for War and a Time for Peace
scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: The poem's second half — stones, embracing, keeping, tearing, silence — closing on love, hate, war, and peace.

scenes.scene_name: He Has Set Eternity in Their Hearts
scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: God making everything beautiful in its time, yet man unable to fathom His work from beginning to end.
The refrain renewed: enjoyment as God's gift, and the enduring works of God that men should fear.

scenes.scene_name: Wickedness in the Place of Judgment
scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: Injustice observed where righteousness should be, with the assurance that God will judge and test men.

scenes.scene_name: Men and Beasts Share One Breath
scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: The leveling enigma of death — all from dust, all to dust — so nothing is better than to enjoy one's work.
The oppressed who have no comforter, leading him to admire the dead and the unborn above the living.

scenes.scene_name: The Vanity of Toil and Solitude
scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: Labor born of envy, the self-consuming fool, and the lonely man who toils with no one to enjoy it.
The praise of companionship: two better than one, and the threefold cord not quickly broken.
Better a poor wise youth than an old foolish king, yet even the new favorite is soon forgotten.

stories.story_title: Observations on Wisdom, Wealth, and Justice
stories.why_start_end_and_literary_glue: A second observation collection (5:1–8:17) ranging from reverent worship to wealth's futility, 'better-than' proverbs, and the enigma of justice. The throughline is what is 'good' for man and the unsearchability of God's works. Ends climactically with man's inability to find out all that God does (8:17).

scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: Reverence at the house of God: draw near to listen, for God is in heaven and you are on earth.
Better not to vow than to vow and not pay; do not let your mouth make your flesh sin — 'fear God.'

scenes.scene_name: He Who Loves Money Is Never Satisfied
scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: Oppression in the bureaucracy, and the insatiable craving of the lover of money and wealth.

scenes.scene_name: Wealth Hoarded to the Owner's Harm
scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: The consumers who multiply with goods, the sleepless rich, and wealth lost in a failed venture.

scenes.scene_name: Naked He Came, Naked He Departs
scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: Taking nothing for his labor, the man who eats all his days in darkness, sorrow, and anger.

scenes.scene_name: Enjoyment Is a Gift from God
scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: The refrain: God's gift of riches and the joy that keeps a man occupied so he seldom counts his days.
The grievous evil of wealth a man cannot enjoy — a stillborn child better off than the unsatisfied man.
The never-satisfied appetite, the wise man's slight advantage, and who can know what is good or what comes after.
The 'better-than' proverbs begin: a good name, the day of death, and the wise heart at home in mourning.
A wise man's rebuke better than the song of fools, and the corruption of extortion and bribery.

scenes.scene_name: The End Is Better Than the Beginning
scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: A patient spirit over a proud one, and the folly of pining for 'the old days.'
Wisdom a sheltering inheritance; in prosperity be joyful, in adversity consider that God made both.
The puzzle of the perishing righteous and the long-lived wicked, and the balance the God-fearer keeps.

scenes.scene_name: No One on Earth Who Never Sins
scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: Wisdom stronger than ten rulers, the universality of sin, and not heeding every overheard word.
His resolve to be wise that proved out of reach — 'what exists is very deep; who can fathom it?'
The snare-woman more bitter than death, and the conclusion that men have sought out many schemes.
Wisdom that brightens the face, and prudence before the supreme word of the king.

scenes.scene_name: No One Has Power Over the Day of Death
scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: A right time and procedure for everything, yet no power over the wind, death, or the release of wickedness.

scenes.scene_name: It Will Go Well with Those Who Fear God
scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: The praised burial of the wicked and delayed sentences, yet the assurance of good for the reverent.
The futility of reversed justice, the commendation of enjoyment, and the unfathomable work done under the sun.

stories.story_title: The Final Exhortation in Light of Certain Death
stories.why_start_end_and_literary_glue: A concluding exhortation (9:1–12:7): since one fate (death) happens to all, live joyfully, act despite uncertainty, rejoice yet remember judgment, and 'remember your Creator' before the dark days. Culminates in the allegory of old age and death (12:1-7).

scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: All in God's hands, yet one fate for righteous and wicked alike — 'a live dog is better than a dead lion.'
Eat your bread with joy, enjoy your wife, and work with all your might, for in Sheol there is no labor.

scenes.scene_name: Time and Chance Happen to All
scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: The race not to the swift; men ensnared like fish or birds in an evil time that suddenly falls.
The poor wise man who saved a city yet was forgotten — 'wisdom is better than weapons of war.'
Dead flies spoiling perfume, the fool exposed on the road, and calmness that lays great offenses to rest.
The error from the ruler: folly exalted to high places while princes go on foot.

scenes.scene_name: He Who Digs a Pit May Fall In
scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: The hazards of work, the dull axe needing more strength, and the snake that bites before charming.
Gracious words of the wise against the fool whose talk begins in folly and ends in madness.
Woe to the land with a feasting youth-king; the cost of laziness; and the bird that carries your words.

scenes.scene_name: Cast Your Bread upon the Waters
scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: The call to bold, diversified action despite uncertainty, sowing seed without knowing which will prosper.
Light is sweet; rejoice in youth — yet know that God will bring you to judgment, for youth is fleeting.

scenes.scene_name: Remember Your Creator in Your Youth
scenes.why_start_end_and_devices: The closing allegory begins: remember Him before the days of adversity and the darkening of the light.
The failing body as a decaying house — trembling keepers, dimming windows, the almond tree, the eternal home.
Death imaged as a broken cord, bowl, and wheel — 'the dust returns to the ground and the spirit to God.'
